# M3.2 quest observation performance research

Researched on 22 September 2026 (host-local date). Target: ATM10 8.2, Minecraft 1.21.1, NeoForge 21.1.251, Java 21, FTB Quests **2101.1.36**, FTB Library 2101.1.36, and FTB Teams 2101.1.11. Research used the exact local adapter, previously retrieved official version-pinned sources, and the installed FTB JAR. It did not interact with the game UI, change the instance, or inspect player saves. Repaired build and runtime results belong in the verification report.

## Observed problem

During the actual M3.1 integrated-server playtest, `/companion next` twice reported `FTB quest observation exceeded the cooperative 250 ms collection budget`. The relevant log timestamps were 22:53:05 and 22:53:52 on 22 September. The same startup log reported **11 chapter groups, 66 chapters and 4,790 quests**. This was a real supported-version book exceeding the observer's work budget, not an absent-mod or unsupported-version failure. No incomplete book was reported as complete.

The adapter collected and validated the entire book for each request. `QuestService.capability(player)` also called `snapshot(player)`, so merely asking whether the integration was available performed the same expensive collection. A lightweight API-readiness observation can avoid that work, provided its detail explicitly distinguishes readiness from successful full-book collection.

The failure text identifies the limit reached; the original adapter did not record a per-phase profile. It therefore does not prove which allocation or API call caused either particular timeout.

## Avoidable work in the supported release

The authoritative source is [FTB Quests v2101.1.36](https://github.com/FTBTeam/FTB-Quests/tree/v2101.1.36), commit `8c53f35a97d8897c861b097f1e39f4fc3beb3a15`. Local source references below are to that revision.

| Source | Finding | Safe optimization |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `QuestObjectBase.getCodeString(long)`, line 82 | Calls `String.format("%016X", id)` every time. The instance method at line 248 delegates to it. There is no cached formatted ID. | Java 21 `HexFormat.of().withUpperCase().toHexDigits(long)` gives the same fixed-width 16-character uppercase hexadecimal representation, including zero and negative signed longs. Compare boundary values and random IDs against the pinned FTB implementation in tests. |
| Companion `QuestSnapshot.id` and `registryId` | `String.matches` compiles a regex for each validated field. IDs recur across quests, tasks, dependencies and chapter references. | Reuse immutable precompiled patterns, or use an equivalent bounded character check. Keep all original rejection semantics. |
| Companion snapshot assembly | Repeatedly allocates identical explanations for unsupported dependency operators and item-task matching. It sorts and copies small nested collections and validates the final book again. | Reuse immutable constants and reduce unnecessary allocation without removing validation or limits. |
| `QuestObjectBase.getTitle()` | The returned title component is cached by FTB; conversion to text still occurs per observation. A quest title can fall back to a task title. Cold lookup also formats translation keys internally, as detailed below. | Keep public title APIs and bounded text. Do not substitute translated display strings for stable IDs, or cache titles across edits without a valid invalidation contract. |
| Minecraft `ItemStack.getComponentsPatch()` | Calls `PatchedDataComponentMap.asPatch()`, which can construct a patch object. Only emptiness is needed for the item-reference flag. | The exact Minecraft 1.21.1 source exposes public `isComponentsPatchEmpty()`, which directly checks the underlying patch and handles empty stacks identically. |
| Companion `QuestService.capability` | Uses full snapshot collection as a readiness check. | Introduce a separate inexpensive readiness probe behind the same optional-version/linkage gate. |

The implementation agent also measured a synthetic DTO-only construction experiment using a fresh Java 21 `jshell -q --class-path ATM-Companion/build/classes/java/main` process. IDs were formatted before timing; the timed work constructed 4,790 quest records, 9,580 task records, one chapter and the final validating snapshot, with empty dependencies and shared immutable observations. It took 383.1 ms on the first call, then 97.6, 69.8, 52.4, 32.6 and 37.2 ms. These diagnostic measurements were reported by the implementation agent; no machine-readable benchmark artifact was retained. They support checking allocation first, but invoke no FTB/Minecraft APIs, are not live ATM10 latency, and cannot establish a repaired runtime result.

Relevant official source: [QuestObjectBase](https://github.com/FTBTeam/FTB-Quests/blob/v2101.1.36/common/src/main/java/dev/ftb/mods/ftbquests/quest/QuestObjectBase.java).

### Remaining cold-title path

An intermediate optimized large-fixture run still exceeded the deadline on its first observation, while later observations completed. This prompted a deeper source investigation rather than treating warmed timings as sufficient evidence.

The exact installed FTB JAR's `TranslationManager.makeKey(QuestObjectBase, TranslationKey)` bytecode invokes both `QuestObjectBase.getCodeString(object)` and `String.format("%s.%s.%s", ...)`. The former invokes `%016X` formatting. `getStringTranslation` calls this private helper, and `QuestObjectBase.getRawTitle` calls `getStringTranslation`. An uncached `getTitle` checks `getRawTitle()` and, when nonempty, calls it again to construct the literal server title. Therefore an uncached object title entails two formatter calls for an absent raw title, or four for a nonempty raw title, before any fallback-specific work. Subsequent `getTitle` calls use FTB's cached component and skip these lookups.

`ItemTask.getAltTitle` constructs a count prefix and appends the configured stack's hover name. Its progress maximum is a simple count getter; `TeamData.getProgress` is a direct map lookup. These source facts make title initialization a plausible cold-path cost, but do not assign a measured proportion without a profile.

There is no public preformatted-key lookup in the live `TranslationManager`: public string/list/entry lookups all invoke `makeKey`, and its table map/accessor are private. Calling a private method, substituting raw pack files, or bypassing a custom task's title semantics is not a clean optimization. A narrower command-specific observation may instead collect current flags and only the titles/details that the command displays. Such a projection must have an explicit schema and must not be presented as a complete detailed book.

The Minecraft component-method evidence comes from `net/minecraft/world/item/ItemStack.java` in the build's exact `neoforge-21.1.251-sources.jar`; FTB translation evidence was checked with `javap -c -p` against the installed `ftb-quests-neoforge-2101.1.36.jar`.

The limited JFR profile contained only 15 adapter-stack samples and did not establish title formatting as a dominant measured cost. The source call chain is confirmed; its share of the actual timeout remains unquantified.

### Selected command scope

The final repair introduces a separate `QuestOverview` for normal `/companion quests` and `/companion next` requests. These commands display current completion/availability counts and at most five available options; they do not need every task title, configured item, dependency edge and progress value. The overview reads current server-side flags, applies the same FTB availability predicates, and formats only the selected option titles. Its schema explicitly states which details were not collected.

Detailed snapshot collection remains available to the debug routes, with its original structural caps and 250 ms cooperative deadline. It may still report unavailable for a cold or expensive full-book collection. This distinction is a deliberate observation-scope boundary, not a cached-progress shortcut or a larger timeout. The revised runtime test must exercise the overview before warming the detailed book, compare it with an independently successful full snapshot, and preserve explicit unavailable semantics for full requests that time out.

## Why a live-progress cache is not justified by these APIs

There is no public monotonic revision covering all observed `TeamData` fields in the pinned release. Its private `shouldSave` flag is a persistence dirty flag: `markDirty()` sets it, and saving resets it. It is neither a public version token nor a durable mutation count.

Started/completed events do not cover every change needed by the observation:

- `setProgress` can change partial task progress without starting or completing the task. It marks dirty and sends a progress packet; the start/completion event paths are conditional.
- `resetProgress` removes progress and marks dirty without a general progress-change event.
- `setStarted` and `setCompleted` update their maps through a private helper. That helper clears caches, marks dirty and sends network messages, rather than providing a universal public revision.
- `setLocked` changes the team lock, cached progress and dirty state independently of start/completion events.
- `mergeData` and `copyData` copy progression maps as teams change.
- `canStartTasks` also consults repeatable-quest cooldowns. `getMilliSecondsUntilRepeatable` uses `System.currentTimeMillis()`, so eligibility can change without a map mutation or event.

Definition-cache events do not repair this gap. `BaseQuestFile.clearCachedData()` emits `ClearFileCacheEvent`, but object editing can clear only the edited object's cache and mark the file dirty. `QuestObjectBase.editedFromGUIOnServer()` is empty in this release; it does not guarantee a full-file cache event. A quest file may reload into the same object. `getAllObjects()` creates an unmodifiable collection wrapper, so comparing wrapper identity is not a definition revision. `getAllChapters()` builds a new list as well.

`TeamData.serializeNBT()` would copy substantially more information than needed, including team/player identity and reward data, while adding sorting and ID-formatting work. `copyData` omits repeatable timing/completion-count maps, so it is not a complete frozen clone for evaluating live availability. Neither is an appropriate shortcut to truthful cheap snapshots.

A multi-tick collector would consequently need an explicit observation window and staleness semantics, or a reliable immutable capture of every consulted field. Calling its mixed-time results current would be incorrect. The narrow repair should first reduce same-request work and keep reading current server-side team data each time.

Relevant official sources: [TeamData](https://github.com/FTBTeam/FTB-Quests/blob/v2101.1.36/common/src/main/java/dev/ftb/mods/ftbquests/quest/TeamData.java), [BaseQuestFile](https://github.com/FTBTeam/FTB-Quests/blob/v2101.1.36/common/src/main/java/dev/ftb/mods/ftbquests/quest/BaseQuestFile.java), and [Quest](https://github.com/FTBTeam/FTB-Quests/blob/v2101.1.36/common/src/main/java/dev/ftb/mods/ftbquests/quest/Quest.java).

## Readiness probe and truth boundaries

A probe can safely check the supported installed version, server-thread access, a server-side quest file that is not loading, a ready FTB Teams manager belonging to the same Minecraft server, the player's current team, and existing nullable team progress. It must use `getNullableTeamData`, not `getOrCreateTeamData` or another method that manufactures progression. Synthetic-player handling stays explicit. The absent-mod path must remain `not_integrated` before optional classes are instantiated.

Successful readiness means the adapter can attempt collection. It does **not** establish that the full book fits size/time limits, that no quests exist, or that a previous cached book is current. Commands requiring quest state still need an actual observation, and must report its unavailable reason if collection fails.

The existing interpretation of quests remains unchanged: progression belongs to the current FTB team; candidate IDs are deterministic rather than ranked; availability combines visible chapter, visible quest, unlocked team, FTB `canStartTasks` and not-completed flags. Dependency operator semantics and task-specific matching remain explicitly unavailable where the API is not integrated.

## Required performance and regression evidence

- Keep the 250 ms cooperative collection budget and structural caps. Check the budget after final snapshot construction/validation as well as during traversal, so expensive final work cannot publish a result outside the measured budget. A cooperative deadline cannot preempt one expensive third-party call or a JVM pause; do not advertise a hard latency guarantee.
- Preserve exact 16-digit uppercase IDs, immutable DTOs, deterministic ordering, current team resolution and nullable progress semantics.
- Demonstrate that a readiness probe does not invoke whole-book collection, and that absent, unsupported and broken integrations retain their distinct safe statuses.
- Exercise a representative large book using real pinned FTB objects and APIs, including cold and repeated observations. Record actual object counts and durations; do not substitute a tiny successful fixture for the 4,790-quest failure case.
- Verify fresh partial progress, completion, lock and team changes remain visible on subsequent observations, with no cross-request progress cache.
- Run existing pure and real-FTB regression tests, then repeat the actual ATM10 command that timed out. Build success or a synthetic benchmark alone does not verify the user's integrated-server fix.

This document records the diagnosis and constraints. Completed automated and isolated official-pack results are recorded separately in `M3.2-ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW.md` and `VERIFICATION.md`; they must remain distinct from the user's integrated-world playtest.
